passages.title: Buffering of arterial plasma
paragraphs: Arterial plasma is held within roughly 0.04 pH units of 7.40 despite a daily acid load of 50–100 mmol of non-volatile acid. The dominant buffer is the carbon dioxide / bicarbonate pair, whose behaviour is described by pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PCO₂)), where bicarbonate is in mmol/L and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is in mmHg. The factor 0.03 converts PCO₂ to the concentration of dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L.

A buffer resists pH change most strongly when the pH of the solution equals the pKa of the buffering pair, because the two forms are then present in equal amounts. The apparent pKa of this pair is 6.1, more than a full unit below the pH it is asked to defend, and in a closed container a buffer this far from its pKa would be a poor one.

What rescues it is that the system is not closed. Dissolved CO₂ is in equilibrium with alveolar gas, and the respiratory centre adjusts ventilation in response to arterial pH and PCO₂ within minutes. Acid added to plasma is converted to CO₂ and breathed off, so the denominator of the ratio is actively held down rather than rising as acid accumulates. The kidney adjusts the numerator over hours to days by reclaiming filtered bicarbonate and excreting ammonium.
Researchers measured arterial blood gases in four patients presenting to an emergency department, shown in Table 1. Reference ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, PCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, and bicarbonate 22–26 mmol/L.

passages.title: Temperature dependence of a hydrolysis reaction
paragraphs: The rate constant of most reactions varies with temperature according to k = A exp(-Eₐ/RT), where Eₐ is the activation energy, R is 8.314 J/(mol K) and T is the absolute temperature. Taking logarithms gives ln k = ln A - Eₐ/(RT), so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line whose gradient is -Eₐ/R.

A research group studied the hydrolysis of a phosphate ester that is also a substrate of alkaline phosphatase. The uncatalysed reaction was followed at five temperatures between 288 K and 328 K in buffer at pH 8.0, and the enzyme-catalysed reaction was followed at 310 K. From the uncatalysed data the group reported an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol. With enzyme present the apparent activation energy fell to 25 kJ/mol, while the measured pre-exponential factor was unchanged within error.

A second group repeated the enzyme-catalysed measurement between 310 K and 340 K and found that the rate rose with temperature to a maximum near 320 K and then fell sharply, even though substrate was still in large excess.

passages.title: Flow through a narrowed artery
paragraphs: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube, the volume flow rate is Q = (π r⁴ ΔP) / (8 η L), where r is the radius, ΔP the pressure difference across the length L, and η the viscosity. Because the radius is raised to the fourth power, small changes in calibre have large consequences for flow at a fixed driving pressure.

Where a vessel narrows, the volume passing any cross-section per second must be the same on both sides of the narrowing, so A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂. Bernoulli's relation then requires that the faster-moving fluid inside the narrowing be at lower pressure: P + (1/2) ρ v² + ρ g h is constant along a streamline for an ideal fluid.

A clinician images a coronary artery and finds a segment where the lumen area has fallen to 40% of the value in the adjacent healthy vessel. Blood velocity in the healthy segment is 0.30 m/s. Take the density of blood as 1060 kg/m³ and treat the vessel as horizontal.

passages.title: Correcting the optics of the eye
paragraphs: A thin lens obeys 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ, and its power in dioptres is P = 1/f with f in metres. Lens powers in contact add, so a corrective lens placed in front of the eye adds its power to that of the eye itself. A converging lens has positive power; a diverging lens has negative power.

The unaided eye focuses light from a range of distances between its near point and its far point. In a myopic eye the far point is closer than infinity, so distant objects cannot be brought to a focus on the retina. In presbyopia the near point recedes with age as the lens stiffens, so close work becomes impossible even though distance vision may be unaffected.

A patient is found to have a far point of 40 cm and, at a later visit some years on, a near point of 66.7 cm. A technician in the same clinic assembles a compound microscope from an objective of focal length 4.0 mm and an eyepiece of focal length 25 mm, with the tube length arranged so that the objective forms an image 160 mm beyond its focal point.

questions.stem: Using the relationship in the passage, what is the plasma pH of Patient W?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 24 / (0.03 × 40) = 24 / 1.2 = 20, and log 20 = log 2 + 1 = 1.30. Adding that to the pKa of 6.1 gives 7.40 - the value the passage names as normal, which is the fastest way to confirm the arithmetic without a calculator.

wrong.A: 7.10 is what you get if the ratio is 10 rather than 20, which would require a PCO₂ of 80 mmHg.
wrong.B: 7.26 does not follow from any pairing of the values given; it is roughly what you get by taking log 15, which no part of the calculation produces.
wrong.D: 7.55 overshoots because log 20 is 1.30, not 1.45. Remember log 2 = 0.30, so log 20 = 1.30 exactly.

questions.stem: Patient X is acidotic. What is this patient's plasma pH?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 12 / (0.03 × 24) = 12 / 0.72 = 16.7. Since log 16.7 falls between log 10 and log 20, the pH must fall between 7.10 and 7.40, which already eliminates two choices. Taking log 16.7 as about 1.22 gives 6.1 + 1.22 = 7.32.

wrong.A: 7.22 would need a ratio of about 13, which means dividing 12 by 0.9 rather than by 0.72.
wrong.C: 7.42 is above the normal value, but this patient has lost more bicarbonate proportionally than CO₂, so the ratio and the pH must both fall.
wrong.D: 7.52 describes an alkalosis. Both numbers are below their reference ranges here, and the bicarbonate has fallen by half while PCO₂ has fallen by only 40%.

questions.stem: Which patient's values are most consistent with a primary respiratory problem that the kidney has had time to compensate for?
questions.explanation: Patient Y has a raised PCO₂ (60 mmHg), which is a respiratory disturbance because PCO₂ is set by ventilation, together with a bicarbonate above range (26 mmol/L). Renal compensation is the slow arm of the system described in the passage, so a bicarbonate that has risen to defend the ratio points to a respiratory problem of some standing.

wrong.A: Patient W has entirely normal values and so has no disturbance to compensate for.
wrong.B: Patient X has a low bicarbonate with a low PCO₂, which is a metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation - the reverse of what is asked.
wrong.D: Patient Z has a high bicarbonate with a low PCO₂. The primary problem is the metabolic alkalosis; a kidney compensating for a respiratory problem would not drive bicarbonate to 36 mmol/L.

questions.stem: If a patient's PCO₂ rose from 40 to 80 mmHg while bicarbonate stayed at 24 mmol/L, the plasma pH would:

choices.D: be unchanged, because bicarbonate did not change

questions.explanation: Doubling PCO₂ halves the ratio, and the logarithm of a halved quantity is 0.30 lower, so the pH falls from 7.40 to 7.10. This is worth recognising on sight: every doubling of PCO₂ at fixed bicarbonate costs 0.30 pH units.

wrong.B: 0.60 units would be two doublings - a PCO₂ of 160 mmHg.
wrong.C: The direction is wrong. CO₂ is the acid member of the pair, so more of it lowers the pH.
wrong.D: The pH depends on the ratio of the two, not on bicarbonate alone, so a change in either moves it.

questions.stem: The passage argues that a buffer is most effective when the solution pH equals the buffer pKa, yet the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair buffers plasma well at pH 7.40. The best explanation is that:

choices.A: the apparent pKa of the pair rises to 7.4 at body temperature
choices.B: bicarbonate is present at a far higher concentration than any other plasma buffer
choices.C: ventilation removes the acid member of the pair, so its concentration does not rise as acid is added
choices.D: plasma proteins and phosphate buffer the pH instead, leaving the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair unused

questions.explanation: The passage makes exactly this point: the system is open, and the respiratory centre holds the CO₂ term down rather than letting it climb. Closed-system buffer reasoning, which is where the pKa rule comes from, does not apply when one member is continuously vented.

wrong.A: The passage gives the apparent pKa as 6.1 and does not describe it shifting with temperature; invoking an unstated shift is unnecessary once the open system is recognised.
wrong.B: Bicarbonate's concentration contributes to buffer capacity, but a high concentration of a buffer far from its pKa still buffers poorly. Concentration alone does not resolve the paradox the passage raises.
wrong.D: Both do contribute, but the passage identifies the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair as dominant, so an explanation that sidelines it contradicts the text.

questions.stem: What does the gradient of a plot of ln k against 1/T give for the uncatalysed reaction?

choices.A: -Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about -6.0 × 10³ K
choices.B: -Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about -4.2 × 10² K
choices.C: +Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about +6.0 × 10³ K
choices.D: ln A, which is independent of temperature

questions.explanation: The passage gives the gradient as -Eₐ/R. With Eₐ = 50 000 J/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol K), Eₐ/R = 6.0 × 10³ K, so the gradient is -6.0 × 10³ K. The sign is negative because the rate rises as 1/T falls.

wrong.B: 4.2 × 10² K comes from dividing 50 000 by 120 or similar; dividing by 8.314 gives roughly 6000, not 420.
wrong.C: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong. Rearranged, ln k = ln A - Eₐ/(RT), so the coefficient of 1/T carries a minus sign.
wrong.D: ln A is the intercept of this plot, not its gradient.

questions.stem: By approximately what factor does the uncatalysed rate constant increase on warming from 298 K to 310 K?
questions.explanation: The ratio is exp[-(Eₐ/R)(1/310–1/298)]. The bracket is about -1.30 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, and multiplying by Eₐ/R = 6.0 × 10³ K gives an exponent of about +0.78, so the ratio is e⁰.78, roughly 2.2. The familiar rule of thumb that rates roughly double over a 10 degree rise is doing the same arithmetic.

wrong.A: 1.04 is the ratio of the temperatures themselves, 310/298. Rate depends exponentially on 1/T, not linearly on T.
wrong.C: 12 would require an activation energy several times larger than 50 kJ/mol over this interval.
wrong.D: Raising the temperature increases the fraction of collisions carrying at least Eₐ, so the rate constant of an uncatalysed step rises.

questions.stem: Taking the pre-exponential factor as unchanged, by roughly what factor does the enzyme raise the rate at 310 K?
questions.explanation: With A unchanged, the ratio of rate constants is exp[(50 000–25 000)/(R x 310)] = exp(25 000/2577) = exp(9.7), which is about 1.6 × 10⁴. Halving the activation energy does far more than halve the barrier's cost, because it sits in an exponent.

wrong.A: A factor of 2 would follow if rate were proportional to 1/Eₐ. It is not; Eₐ appears in an exponent.
wrong.B: 10² corresponds to an exponent near 4.6, which would need the activation energy to fall by only about 12 kJ/mol.
wrong.D: 10⁶ needs an exponent near 13.8, which would require a drop of about 36 kJ/mol rather than 25.

questions.stem: What best explains the second group's finding that the catalysed rate falls above about 320 K?

choices.A: The activation energy of the catalysed reaction rises with temperature
choices.B: The enzyme denatures, so the concentration of functional catalyst falls
choices.C: The reaction becomes endothermic above 320 K
choices.D: Substrate becomes limiting at higher temperature

questions.explanation: Arrhenius behaviour predicts a monotonic rise, so a fall means the catalyst itself is being lost. Above a protein's melting range the tertiary structure unfolds and the active site is destroyed, and that loss outruns the Arrhenius gain.

wrong.A: Activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway, and treating it as temperature-dependent here invents a mechanism when a much simpler one fits.
wrong.C: Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is a thermodynamic property that does not flip at a particular temperature, and in any case it sets the position of equilibrium rather than the rate.
wrong.D: The passage states that substrate was still in large excess, so saturation cannot explain the fall.

questions.stem: Independently of the case described, if disease narrowed a vessel's radius by 20% at a fixed pressure difference, flow through it would fall to approximately:
questions.explanation: Flow goes as r⁴, so the fraction remaining is 0.8⁴ = 0.41. This is the single most useful consequence of Poiseuille's relation: a fifth off the radius costs nearly 60% of the flow.

wrong.A: 80% treats flow as proportional to radius. The fourth power is the whole point of the relation.
wrong.B: 64% is 0.8³, which would be the answer if flow went as r³.
wrong.D: 20% confuses the fraction lost from the radius with the fraction of flow remaining.

questions.stem: What is the blood velocity inside the narrowed segment?
questions.explanation: Continuity applies to area, and the passage gives the area as 40% of healthy. So v₂ = v₁ x (A₁/A₂) = 0.30 × (1/0.40) = 0.75 m/s. Note that the area ratio is used once: squaring it would be appropriate only if the passage had given a radius ratio.

wrong.A: 0.12 m/s multiplies by 0.40 instead of dividing by it, which would have fluid slowing down as the vessel narrows - impossible if the same volume must pass each second.
wrong.C: 1.9 m/s squares the area ratio, giving 2.5² = 6.25. That step converts a radius ratio into an area ratio, but the passage has already given the area.
wrong.D: 4.7 m/s raises the ratio to the fourth power, which belongs to the flow-versus-radius relation and not to continuity.

questions.stem: Approximately how much lower is the pressure inside the narrowed segment than in the healthy vessel?
questions.explanation: For a horizontal vessel Bernoulli gives ΔP = (1/2) ρ (v₂² - v₁². With v₁ = 0.30 m/s and v₂ = 0.75 m/s, that is 0.5 × 1060 × (0.5625–0.09) = 2.5 × 10² Pa, which is under 2 mmHg - small, because these velocities are low.

wrong.A: 48 Pa is the dynamic pressure of the healthy segment alone, 0.5 × 1060 × 0.30². It leaves out the faster fluid inside the narrowing, which is where the pressure actually falls.
wrong.C: 1.8 × 10³ Pa follows from taking the velocity in the narrowing as 1.9 m/s, which comes from squaring an area ratio the passage had already given as an area.
wrong.D: 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa is roughly two atmospheres. A sanity check against arterial pressures, which span about 1.3 × 10⁴ Pa, rules it out immediately.

questions.stem: The passage's flow relation assumes a rigid tube. A real artery is elastic, and the pressure inside the narrowed segment is lower than outside it. Compared with the rigid-tube prediction, flow through the diseased segment should therefore be:

choices.A: lower, because the drop in internal pressure tends to collapse the segment further
choices.B: higher, because an elastic wall stores energy and returns it to the fluid
choices.C: identical, because Bernoulli's relation already accounts for wall elasticity
choices.D: higher, because elastic walls reduce the effective viscosity of blood

questions.explanation: Bernoulli requires lower pressure where the fluid moves faster, and a compliant wall responds to a lower internal pressure by narrowing further. That reduces the radius, which by the fourth-power relation reduces flow below the rigid-tube prediction - a self-reinforcing effect that matters clinically.

wrong.B: Elastic storage redistributes energy over the cardiac cycle but does not add energy, and the question asks about the steady narrowing rather than pulsatile recoil.
wrong.C: Bernoulli's relation is written for an ideal fluid in a fixed geometry and says nothing about how the wall responds.
wrong.D: Viscosity is a property of the blood, not of the wall.

questions.stem: What power of corrective lens does the patient need to see distant objects clearly?
questions.explanation: The lens must take light from infinity and make it appear to come from the far point, 40 cm in front of the eye, which means a virtual image at -0.40 m. Then P = 1/(-0.40) = -2.5 D. The negative sign is the useful check: myopia is always corrected with a diverging lens.

wrong.B: -0.4 D inverts the arithmetic, using 0.40 m directly rather than its reciprocal.
wrong.C: +0.4 D has both the magnitude and the sign wrong.
wrong.D: +2.5 D has the right magnitude but a converging lens would move the far point closer still, making distance vision worse.

questions.stem: At the later visit, what additional power is needed to let the patient read at 25 cm?
questions.explanation: The reading lens must take an object at 25 cm and form an image at the near point, 66.7 cm, so P = 1/0.25–1/0.667 = 4.0–1.5 = +2.5 D. Working in dioptres rather than centimetres keeps this to one subtraction.

wrong.A: +1.5 D is the 1/0.667 term on its own, which is the power the eye can already manage.
wrong.C: +4.0 D is the 1/0.25 term on its own and ignores what the eye still does unaided.
wrong.D: +5.5 D adds the two terms instead of subtracting, which would overcorrect substantially.

questions.stem: The image the objective of the microscope forms is best described as:
questions.explanation: The objective is a converging lens with the specimen just outside its focal length, so it forms a real, inverted image inside the tube. That real image then serves as the object for the eyepiece, which magnifies it as a virtual image.

wrong.B: A single converging lens forming a real image always inverts it.
wrong.C: The image is formed inside the tube where it can act as a real object for the eyepiece, so it is real rather than virtual.
wrong.D: Virtual and upright describes what the eyepiece produces, not the objective.

questions.stem: Taking the near point of the relaxed eye as 25 cm, the approximate total magnification of the microscope is:
questions.explanation: The objective contributes image distance over focal length, 160 / 4.0 = 40x. The eyepiece acts as a magnifier contributing 250 / 25 = 10x with both lengths in millimetres. Multiplying gives about 400x.

wrong.B: 100x would need an eyepiece contribution of 2.5x rather than 10x.
wrong.D: 4000x comes from a factor-of-ten slip, most often from mixing millimetres and centimetres in the eyepiece term.
